paragraphs: The robot never worked. That is the honest summary of my sophomore year. I spent seven months on a line-following car that could not follow a line, and I want to explain why that matters to me.

My design was bad from the start. I used two cheap IR sensors mounted too close together, maybe four centimetres apart, because that was what fit on the breadboard I already owned. When the car hit a curve the sensors both read the same value and the controller just guessed. I did not know the phrase "insufficient sensor separation" then. I only knew that my car drove into a wall in front of forty people at the regional meet, and that the kid from Central High laughed.

I rebuilt it. Not immediately, though. I put the whole thing in a shoebox under my bed for about six weeks and told my mom I was done with robotics. Then in January I got bored and pulled it out again, and this time I actually read the sensor datasheet instead of guessing. Four centimetres was wrong. Eleven was better. I also learned that my PID loop had no derivative term at all, which is a little embarrassing to admit in writing.

The car placed fourth in April. Not first. Fourth. But it finished the course three times out of three, and when it did I remember standing there with my hands in my pockets feeling something that was not exactly pride. It was more like relief, the specific relief of a thing that finally does what you told it to do. I still chase that feeling. It is the reason I want to study mechanical engineering, and it is a stupid reason, but it is mine.

There is a particular sound that a flat-top griddle makes at 5:40 in the morning, before anything is on it. A low tick as the metal expands. My father calls it the restaurant waking up. I have heard that sound almost every Saturday since I was nine.

Our diner has eleven tables and one booth that nobody wants because the vinyl is cracked. My job used to be lemons. Just lemons - slice them, quarter them, load them into the little steel bin. Then it was coffee. Then it was the register, which was terrifying, because the register meant talking to Mr. Alvarez who orders the same three eggs every week and gets upset if the plate is warm.

What I did not expect was to love the tickets. The paper slips come off the printer in a rhythm and you learn to read the whole morning off them - two omelettes and a short stack means the church crowd is early, a lone black coffee at 6:15 means somebody had a hard night. My father can look at a rail of tickets and know, without counting, whether we will make rent that month. I have watched him do it. He does not explain how.

I am not going to say the restaurant taught me discipline, because that is what everyone says and it flattens it. What it actually taught me is that a place can hold a family together in a very literal, load-bearing way. When my aunt got sick in 2022, the diner paid for it. Eleven tables and a cracked booth paid for it. I want to study economics because I want to understand the machinery of that, the part my father knows by feel and I want to know by name.
My grandmother forgot my name on a Tuesday in October. She called me by my mother's name instead, and then, when I corrected her, she looked embarrassed and asked me to pass the salt.

The word the neurologist used was vascular. Not Alzheimer's, which is what everyone assumes. Small strokes, dozens of them, too small to notice individually. She had been having them for maybe two years. Nobody caught it because she is stubborn and because she has always mixed up names, even before, even when she was fifty and sharp.

I became the one who sat with her on Thursdays. This was not noble. My brother had baseball and I had nothing, so it was me. We watched cooking shows. She cannot follow a plot anymore but she can follow a recipe, and she would narrate the steps a half second before the host did, like a person singing along to a song from before the war. Fold, she would say. Now fold. She was almost always right.

I have read that the last thing to go is procedural memory. The hands remember. I do not know if that is comforting or not. What I know is that I want to study neuroscience, and I am aware that this is a cliché - the grandchild who watched someone disappear and now wants to fix it. I do not think I will fix it. I would like to be in the room where people are trying.
I lost a debate round in November because I did not know what the word "fiat" meant. I had heard it maybe thirty times that season and I had been nodding confidently the entire time.

Here is what happened. My opponent, a junior from Weston with a binder the size of a car battery, said the word, and I said something back that sounded relevant, and the judge wrote a comment on the ballot that I still have. It said: "Aff does not appear to understand the objection." Four words of that sentence are doing a lot of work.

So I went and learned it. Badly at first - I read a forum post from 2009 and got more confused. Then my coach sat me down and explained it in about ninety seconds, and I felt the specific hot shame of realizing that I could have asked any adult in that building at any point in the previous four months. I just did not want to be the kid who did not know.

That is the actual thing I got out of debate, and it is not eloquence, which is what the trophies imply. It is that I now ask. I ask in chemistry when I do not follow the mechanism. I asked my boss at the pool what a chemical log sheet was for, out loud, in front of two lifeguards. It is a small skill. It cost me one round and a comment I have not thrown away.

When I came to United States I was twelve years old and I did not know how to say "I don't understand" in a way that sounded polite. So for three months I said only "okay." Teachers thought I understood everything. I understood almost nothing.

My family came from Tashkent. In Uzbekistan I was good student, top of class in mathematics, and here I was placed in the class for students who are learning English, which also was the class where they gave us worksheets about colors. I was thirteen and I was writing the word "orange" on a line. I remember feeling that my brain was being wasted, and also feeling ashamed for thinking this, because my parents were working two jobs each and they did not complain.

The thing that changed was the library. There is a librarian named Mrs. Okafor and she did not simplify her words for me, which at first was very difficult and then was the only reason I learned anything. She gave me books that were too hard. She said, read it and come back and tell me one thing. Not all things. One thing. I did this for two years.

Now I read faster in English than in Russian, which is strange and a little sad. I want to study computer science. I mention my English not because I want sympathy for it but because I know what it is to hold a complicated thought and not have the words yet. It makes me patient with people who are in the middle of that. I think this is useful in any team.
4:45 a.m. Practice at 5:15. Six days a week for eleven years. That is roughly 3,400 mornings, though I have never actually counted and I am not going to now.

I was never the fastest. I want to be clear about that up front because a lot of these essays are secretly about winning. I swam the 500 free and I was, at my absolute peak, the third-fastest girl on a mid-table team in a mid-table conference. My best time was 5:21.86. The state cut was 5:11. I never got it. I am telling you the number because the number is the point.

What eleven years of not quite getting there does to a person is interesting. For a while it made me bitter - sophomore year I was genuinely unpleasant to be around, and my teammate Nadia told me so in the locker room in words I will not repeat. She was right. Then something shifted. I started coaching the eight-and-unders on Saturday mornings, which was supposed to be a service requirement and became the best part of my week. There is a kid named Theo who is afraid of the deep end and who now jumps in without stopping at the edge. I did that. Not the 5:11.

I still swim. I will swim in college if a team will have me, and if not I will swim anyway at six in the morning in whatever pool is nearest, because at this point the water is just where I think. I want to study public health. I am interested in the gap between what a body can do and what a body is allowed to do, and I first noticed that gap at the shallow end with a nine-year-old.

The lot on Vine Street was a lot before it was a garden. Broken glass, two shopping carts, a mattress. In April of my freshman year the neighborhood association got a permit and about nine of us showed up with shovels, mostly retirees and me.

We did not know what we were doing. We planted tomatoes too close together and lost most of them to blight. The peppers did fine. Someone donated a raspberry bush that produced exactly four raspberries in three years and became a running joke.

What I actually learned there had nothing to do with plants. Mrs. Petrosian, who is eighty-one, taught me how to run a meeting. Not formally. I just watched her handle a forty-minute argument about whether to allow a compost bin, and she did it by letting the loudest man talk himself out and then asking a quiet question. The bin got built. I have used that trick twice, once in student council and once with my own father.
Fourteen families use the lot now. I do not think I made that happen. I carried a lot of soil, and I showed up on Saturdays for four years, which is a lower bar than it sounds like but not nothing.

I started piano at fifteen, which everyone told me was too late, and they were partly correct. My hands will never be the hands of a person who started at four. There is a physical fact underneath that and I have stopped arguing with it.

My teacher is a retired man named Mr. Sorokin who charges twenty dollars an hour and does not believe in recitals. First lesson, he asked what I wanted to play. I said Chopin, because that is what you say. He laughed at me - not unkindly - and gave me a Bartók piece for children that took me five weeks and made me want to quit twice.

The interesting part is what it did to how I hear things. I now cannot listen to a song without accidentally counting. I noticed the piano in a grocery store commercial was slightly out of tune and said so out loud to nobody. My sister finds this insufferable. But I also hear my own thinking differently - I notice when an argument in an essay resolves too early, the way a phrase resolves too early, and I did not have that before.

I am not going to conservatory. I want to study linguistics, and I think the connection is obvious enough that I do not need to spell it out, except to say that both are about structures that you can feel before you can name. Mr. Sorokin still gives me pieces that are too hard. I still play them badly, and then eventually less badly, which turns out to be the whole thing.
I worked at Sudsy's on Route 9 for two summers. Twelve dollars an hour, mostly the dry line, sometimes the vacuum bay when someone called out.

The job is more skilled than it looks. There is an order to drying a car - roof, glass, hood, trunk, doors, wheels last - and if you break the order you get streaks and the customer comes back and it is your fault. I broke the order constantly for about two weeks. A guy named Dre who had been there nine years fixed my technique in one afternoon by standing behind me and not saying anything until I was wrong.

I also learned what it is like to be looked past. Not at, past. People hand you keys without turning their heads. A woman in a white Lexus told her kid to stop staring at me. That happened in July and I thought about it for the rest of the summer, and I still think about it, and I do not have a tidy paragraph to put after it.

I am the first in my family who will go to college. My mother cleans rooms at the Marriott on Airport Road and she has been looked past for twenty-two years, and she has never once described it to me the way I just described one afternoon. I want to study sociology. Partly I want the vocabulary for what happened in that parking lot. Mostly I want to be someone who turns his head.
My app had four users. Two of them were me, on two different phones, and one was my mother, who I believe opened it once out of obligation.

It was called StudySync and it was supposed to let you see which of your friends were currently studying, so that you would feel guilty and also study. This is, I now understand, a product built on the assumption that shame is a renewable resource. It is not. My friends turned off notifications within a day.

Technically it mostly worked, which is the part I am still proud of. I wrote it in React Native over one winter break, and I did the Firebase auth flow myself after failing at it three times, and there was a moment at two in the morning on December 29th when the presence indicator finally lit up green on both phones and I said something out loud that I will not put in a college essay.

The failure was not technical. I never asked anyone if they wanted this. I built for four months and validated for zero minutes, and when I finally asked my friend Ruth why she stopped using it she said, immediately, without needing to think: "because it made me feel bad and I already feel bad." That sentence rearranged how I think about building things. I want to study human-computer interaction. I would like to spend my career asking Ruth's question first instead of on December 29th.
My brother Ezra is nine and autistic and does not like Tuesdays, because Tuesday is when the recycling truck comes and the sound of the hydraulics is, in his words, wrong in his teeth.

For three years I have handled Tuesday mornings. My parents both leave at 6:30. The routine is specific: headphones on before 7:10, the blue ones not the grey ones, and we go through the trash truck as a script we have written together. First it comes down Fulton. Then it stops at the Kaminskis'. Then the noise, which lasts eleven seconds. Ezra counts them. On a good day he counts them out loud and on a bad day I count them for him.

I want to resist the version of this essay where my brother is a lesson. He is not a lesson, he is a nine-year-old who is very funny about elevators and who beat me at Uno so decisively last month that I suspect cheating. But I have learned things by accident. Mostly I have learned that most systems are built for the median person and that the distance between the median and my brother is where almost all of the suffering is.

I want to study industrial design. Specifically I want to work on the boring end of it - the interfaces on medical devices, the ones nobody photographs. Eleven seconds is a design problem. Someone chose that hydraulic. I would like to be in the room next time.
Third from the left, second row, sousaphone, forty-one pounds of brass strapped to a person who at the time weighed one hundred and twelve.

Band camp is in August in Georgia which is a sentence that should require a warning label, and my first year I passed out on the practice field on day three, and the athletic trainer gave me a bag of pretzels and told me that salt is a nutrient, which nobody had explained to me before in fifteen years of being alive. I got better. By senior year I could do a full run-through in the heat and still count the drill, which sounds small unless you have tried to count sixteen bars while walking backwards.

Here is the thing about marching band that outsiders miss. It is not about music, not really, not while you are doing it. It is about being one of one hundred and forty people who all have to be in exactly the wrong place at exactly the right time. If I am eight inches off, the form bends, and if the form bends the drum major sees it from the tower, and it is visible from the stands. Eight inches. There is nowhere to hide, and I found that clarifying rather than stressful, which apparently says something about me.

I am going to study statistics, and I have thought about why, and I think it is this: I like systems where individual error is measurable and correctable and does not require anyone to be humiliated about it. Mr. Fields never once yelled. He would just say "row two, check your interval," and row two would check its interval, and the form would come back.
In four years of high school I have attended three different schools in two countries. I would like to describe what this does to a person, if I am able.

My father is engineer for pipeline company and his contracts are two years or three years. We moved from Lagos to Houston when I was fourteen, and then from Houston to Calgary when I was sixteen. Each time I am new student in October, which is worst month to be new, because friendships are already decided in September and nobody is looking for another person.

What I developed is a system. It is not beautiful but it works. In first week I do not try to make friends. I find the one activity where they need bodies - in Houston it was the robotics team who needed someone to do wiring, in Calgary it was the school newspaper who needed someone to lay out pages. Nobody refuses a person who is useful. Then after six weeks of being useful you are simply there, and being there is most of friendship.

I am aware this sounds calculating. Maybe it is. But I have also learned that I can be dropped into a room of strangers and be functional within a month, and this is not a small thing, and I did not have it when I was fourteen and cried in a Houston bathroom during lunch period for eleven days. I want to study civil engineering, like my father, but I want to do the part where you decide where the pipeline goes and who it goes past.
There is a bike co-op in the basement of the Unitarian church on Sixth and I have been there almost every Wednesday since eighth grade. Free repairs, donated parts, one very old truing stand.

I am good at wheels. That is my thing. A wheel is thirty-six spokes each pulling against a rim, and if one spoke is too tight the whole thing goes out of true, and the fix is quarter-turns and patience and a lot of spinning it to listen. My record is a rim that was bent almost forty millimetres out and I got it to under one. It took two and a half hours and I could not feel my thumbs.

Mostly though the co-op is people. A man named Terrence comes in with the same seized-up Schwinn every few months and we both know he does not really need help, and that is fine, that is what the co-op is. A woman brought in a child's bike in February and cried a little when we fixed the training wheels for free.

I do not have a grand conclusion. I want to study mechanical engineering. I like objects that tell you what is wrong with them if you know how to listen, and I found out I like that in a church basement with a spoke wrench.
I shelve books at the Brookdale branch on Mondays, Wednesdays, and every other Saturday. The pay is $13.10. The job is quiet and slightly strange and I have thought about it more than I expected to.

Shelving is not sorting. Sorting you can do with a rule. Shelving means holding about forty books in a cart in Dewey order and walking a route through a building, and the interesting part is that the building has a shape and the numbers have a shape and they do not match. The 300s are around a corner. Somebody in 1974 made a decision about a wall and I am paying for it forty years later, thirty seconds at a time, forty times a shift.

The other thing about the job is who is there. The library is where people go when they have nowhere else to be in the middle of a Tuesday. There is a man who comes in at opening and reads the newspaper for four hours and does not have a home, and the librarians know his name, and nobody ever asks him to leave. That policy is not written anywhere. I asked.

I want to study library and information science, which people find funny when I say it at seventeen. But somebody has to decide where the 300s go, and somebody has to decide that a man can sit for four hours, and I have come to believe those are the same kind of decision.
My rating peaked at 1642 in March of junior year and has been slowly declining since, which is a normal thing to happen and a strange thing to watch happen to yourself at sixteen.

I am a positional player, which mostly means I am bad at calculating and have built an entire style around avoiding positions where calculation matters. This is a real weakness and I know it. My coach, who is a 2100 and a chemistry teacher, told me in ninth grade that I would hit a ceiling around 1700 unless I did tactics drills, and he was right, and I did not do the drills.

What chess actually gave me was the habit of writing down my losses. You are supposed to annotate. After every tournament game you go back and mark where it went wrong, and you cannot lie in the notation because the notation is just what happened. I have four notebooks. Game 47 in book two says, in my handwriting, "I knew this was bad and played it anyway because I was tired."

I would like to study mathematics. Partly for the obvious reason. Mostly because I like fields where you are allowed to write down that you were wrong and it is considered a normal part of working, rather than a confession.

I pushed a cart of magazines and warm blankets around the fourth floor of Mercy General for two years. Tuesdays and Sundays. The official title was Patient Comfort Volunteer, which is a generous name for a person who mostly delivered ginger ale.

Nobody prepares you for the boredom. I had imagined something dramatic - I was fifteen, I had watched television - and what it actually is, is a lot of walking on linoleum and a lot of doors where you knock and nobody answers. The dramatic parts happen behind doors you are not allowed to open. Twice in two years I was asked to leave a hallway quickly and both times I found out later what had happened and both times it was a person dying.

The part I did not expect was the families. They are in the hallway because there is nowhere else, and they have been there for nine hours, and they will talk to anyone. A man named Sal told me about his wife's entire career as a school bus driver while we stood next to a vending machine that only took exact change. I do not think he wanted comfort. I think he wanted a witness.

I am going to study nursing. Not medicine - nursing, specifically, and I have had that argument with two relatives. The person in the room the most is the nurse. Sal did not need a diagnosis at 11 p.m. He needed somebody to stand there, and I found out that I can stand there, and that this is a skill that some people do not have.
The first thing I ever cooked alone was scrambled eggs and they were, objectively, wrong. Grey. I was eleven and I had used the heat all the way up because I thought cooking was a race.

My mother works nights at a call center so dinner became mine somewhere around sixth grade, out of logistics rather than passion. For a year and a half we ate pasta with jarred sauce roughly four nights a week. Then my aunt gave me a paperback cookbook from 1988 with a stain on the cover and I read it like a novel, cover to cover, including the section on canning, which I have never done.

The turning point was learning that heat is a variable. That sounds obvious written down. But there is a specific afternoon I remember, standing at our stove with the burner on medium-low, waiting four whole minutes for onions to go translucent instead of brown, and understanding for the first time in my life that patience is a technique and not a personality trait. I made a lot of things after that. Some were bad. The chicken thing in March was actively upsetting.

I feed four people most nights and I am fast now, twenty-five minutes for something real, and I have opinions about knives that I try to keep to myself at parties. I want to study chemical engineering, and yes, I know how that sounds coming after four paragraphs about onions. Heat, time, and a variable you can control. It is the same essay.
